intro: In 1860, most Americans lived on farms, and much of the West belonged to Native nations. By 1920, railroads crossed the continent, more Americans lived in cities than on farms, and the United States ruled lands across the Pacific and the Caribbean. Few times in the nation's history brought so much change so fast.

This unit follows the people who lived through that change. You will meet cowboys, homesteaders and Exodusters, and Plains nations fighting to keep their homelands. You will meet inventors, business giants, factory workers and millions of immigrants. You will see Chicago burn and rise again, and visit Jane Addams at Hull House. Then you will meet the reformers who tried to fix what fast growth had broken, from muckraking reporters to the women who won the vote.

As you read, notice who gained from all this growth and who paid the price. Some people found land, jobs and freedom. Others lost their homes, their rights or their lives. Americans in this era argued hard about what government should do to make the country fair, and those arguments still shape our lives today.
bigQuestion: How did growth in the West, in industry and overseas change who Americans were, and who paid the price for that growth?

story.title: The Buffalo Nearly Vanish
story.kicker: Tens of millions of bison once roamed the Plains. By 1890, only a few hundred were left in the wild.
paragraphs: Picture a sea of brown backs moving across the grass. The herd is so big that it takes days to pass by. The ground shakes under their hooves. For thousands of years, scenes like this were normal on the Great Plains. Tens of millions of American bison, often called buffalo, lived there. No one counted them, but they were one of the largest herds of animals on Earth.

For Plains nations such as the Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche and Kiowa, the buffalo meant life. People ate the meat fresh or dried it for winter. Hides became tipi covers, robes and moccasins. Bones became tools. Horns became cups and spoons. Nothing was wasted. The buffalo also held a sacred place in songs, stories and ceremonies.

Then, in just a few decades, the herds almost disappeared. Railroads cut across the Plains in the 1860s and 1870s. Hunters rode the trains west and shot bison by the thousands. In the 1870s, factories in the East learned to turn buffalo hides into tough leather, so a single hide could be sold for cash. Hunters often skinned the animals and left the meat to rot. Some army leaders were glad to see the herds go. They knew that without the buffalo, Plains nations could not keep their way of life.

By about 1890, only a few hundred wild bison were left. Piles of bleached bones lay across the prairie. Settlers gathered them and sold them by the ton to be ground into fertilizer. A few people began to worry. William Hornaday, a zoo scientist, counted the survivors and warned that the animal could soon be gone forever. A small wild herd hung on in Yellowstone National Park, and a handful of ranchers kept small herds of their own.

Slowly, people worked to bring the bison back. In 1905, a group called the American Bison Society formed, with Theodore Roosevelt as its honorary president. In 1907, bison raised at the Bronx Zoo in New York were sent by train to a preserve in Oklahoma. Over the next century, herds grew on ranches, in parks and on Native lands. Many tribes now raise buffalo again as part of their culture. In 2014, bison returned to Nachusa Grasslands in northern Illinois.

Today, the United States has hundreds of thousands of bison, and in 2016 the bison became the national mammal. Still, they are not the endless herds of the past. The story of the buffalo is the story of the West in small: great wealth and growth for some, and terrible loss for others.
story.think: Why do you think it took so long for people to try to save the bison? Who worked to bring them back, and why?

lessons.title: Mining Booms and Boomtowns
lessons.mainIdea: Discoveries of gold and silver drew thousands of people west and created towns that grew fast and often died just as fast.
reading: The California Gold Rush of 1849 was only the beginning. In 1858 and 1859, gold was found near Pikes Peak in Colorado. In 1859, miners in Nevada struck a huge deposit of silver and gold called the *Comstock Lode*. News spread fast. Thousands of fortune seekers rushed to the mountains, hoping to strike it rich.

Near each strike, a *boomtown* popped up almost overnight. Virginia City, Nevada, grew from a few tents into a busy city with hotels, theaters and newspapers. Merchants, cooks, laundry workers and saloon owners often made more money than the miners did. Women ran boardinghouses and restaurants. Chinese, Mexican, Irish and Cornish miners all worked in the camps, though Chinese and Mexican miners often faced unfair taxes and violence.

Most single miners never got rich. The easy gold near the surface ran out quickly. Digging deep into rock took costly machines, so big mining companies took over. When the ore was gone, many towns emptied out and became *ghost towns*. Mining also brought settlers onto Native lands, which led to conflict across the West.

a town that grows very quickly because of a sudden chance to make money

lessons.title: Rails Across the Continent
lessons.mainIdea: The first transcontinental railroad, finished in 1869, tied East and West together and was built largely by Chinese and Irish workers.
reading: In 1862, during the Civil War, Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act. It gave two companies land and loans to build a railroad across the country. The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, California, and built east. The Union Pacific started in Omaha, Nebraska, and built west. This line would be the first *transcontinental* railroad, meaning it crossed the whole continent.

The Central Pacific had to cut through the steep Sierra Nevada mountains. It hired thousands of Chinese *immigrants*, who soon made up most of its workers. They blasted tunnels through solid granite and worked through deep snow. They were paid less than white workers and had to buy their own food. Many died in accidents and avalanches. On the Union Pacific, many workers were Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans.

On May 10, 1869, the two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah. Leaders tapped in a ceremonial golden spike, and a telegraph message told the nation the job was done. A trip across the country that once took months by wagon now took about a week. More railroads followed. They brought settlers, carried cattle and crops to market, and changed the West forever.

lessons.title: Cattle Drives and Cowboys
lessons.mainIdea: After the Civil War, cowboys of many backgrounds drove Texas cattle north to railroad towns, until fences and hard winters ended the open range.
reading: After the Civil War, millions of longhorn cattle roamed Texas. A steer worth a few dollars in Texas could sell for much more in the North, where cities wanted beef. The answer was the *cattle drive*. Cowboys herded cattle hundreds of miles north to railroad towns in Kansas, such as Abilene. From there, trains carried the cattle to places like the Union Stock Yards in Chicago.

The cowboy's skills came from Mexican *vaqueros*, who had herded cattle for generations. Words like lasso, rodeo and chaps come from Spanish. Cowboys were a mixed group. Many were Mexican or Mexican American. Historians estimate that perhaps one in four was Black, many of them formerly enslaved. Nat Love, a Black cowboy, later wrote a book about his life on the trail.

A drive could take two or three months. Cowboys faced storms, stampedes and river crossings for low pay. The era of long drives lasted only about twenty years. Railroads reached farther into Texas. Farmers fenced their land with *barbed wire*, a cheap fence invented by Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, in 1874. Then the terrible winter of 1886–1887 killed huge numbers of cattle, and the open range came to an end.

lessons.title: Homesteads on the Prairie
lessons.mainIdea: The Homestead Act offered free land, but families who farmed the Plains faced a hard, lonely life with few trees and harsh weather.
reading: In 1862, Congress passed the *Homestead Act*. It offered 160 acres of public land to a settler who would live on it and farm it for five years. The settler paid only a small filing fee. Men, women who headed households, and immigrants who planned to become citizens could all apply. Hundreds of thousands of families, including many from Germany, Norway and Sweden, moved onto the Plains.

The Plains had few trees, so there was little wood for houses. Many settlers cut blocks of thick, grassy soil called sod and stacked them like bricks. These *sod houses* stayed warm in winter and cool in summer, but dirt fell from the ceiling, and snakes and mice sometimes came through the walls. Families burned dried buffalo or cow chips for fuel.

Life was hard. Blizzards, droughts, prairie fires and swarms of grasshoppers could ruin a year's work. Women cooked, sewed, tended gardens, cared for animals and nursed the sick, often miles from the nearest neighbor. Children hauled water and herded animals. New tools helped: steel plows cut the tough sod, and windmills pumped water from deep underground. Still, many homesteaders gave up and moved away.

lessons.title: The Exodusters
lessons.mainIdea: Thousands of Black Southerners moved to Kansas in the late 1870s, seeking land, safety and freedom after Reconstruction ended.
reading: When Reconstruction ended in 1877, life grew more dangerous for Black families in the South. Many were trapped in debt as sharecroppers. White groups used violence to keep them from voting. Many people began to look west for a fresh start. Kansas stood out. It had been a free state, and it had land for homesteading.

In 1879, thousands of Black Southerners traveled to Kansas. They called themselves *Exodusters*, after the Book of Exodus in the Bible, which tells how the Israelites escaped slavery in Egypt. Some came by steamboat up the Mississippi River. Others walked. Benjamin "Pap" Singleton, a formerly enslaved man from Tennessee, encouraged the move and helped start Black settlements.

One all-Black town, Nicodemus, Kansas, was founded in 1877. Its settlers lived in dugouts and sod houses at first. Farming was hard, and many arrived with almost nothing. Still, the Exodusters built churches, schools and farms. Their *migration* showed that freedpeople were willing to risk everything to own land and live with dignity.

lessons.title: Farmers Fight Back
lessons.mainIdea: Farmers facing debt, low prices and high railroad rates joined together in the Grange and later the Populist Party.
reading: By the 1870s, many farmers were in trouble. They grew more crops than ever, so prices fell. Many had borrowed money for land and machines and could not pay it back. Railroads charged high rates to ship their crops, and farmers often had only one railroad to choose from. Farmers felt that banks and railroads held all the power.

Farmers began to organize. The *Grange*, founded in 1867, started as a social club for farm families. It soon pushed states to pass laws limiting railroad and grain storage rates. In the case Munn v. Illinois in 1877, the Supreme Court ruled that a state could regulate businesses that served the public, such as grain warehouses in Chicago.

In 1892, farmers and workers formed the People's Party, also called the *Populist Party*. Populists wanted the government to own the railroads, create an income tax, let voters elect senators directly, and coin more silver money so that farmers could pay off debts more easily. In 1896, Democrat William Jennings Bryan, who was born in Salem, Illinois, ran for president with Populist support. He lost to William McKinley, but many Populist ideas later became law.

lessons.title: The People of the Plains
lessons.mainIdea: Plains nations built their lives around the horse and the buffalo, and the loss of the herds and their land broke their way of life.
reading: Many nations lived on the Great Plains, including the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Kiowa, Crow and Pawnee. Some farmed along rivers. Others moved with the seasons, following the buffalo. After Spanish horses spread north in the 1600s and 1700s, many Plains peoples became skilled riders and hunters.

The buffalo gave Plains families food, clothing, shelter and tools. Plains nations also had their own governments, religions and ways of sharing land. As settlers, miners and railroads moved west, the U.S. government signed treaties with many nations. Treaties promised land that would be theirs forever. Again and again, the promises were broken when settlers wanted the land.

The government pushed Plains nations onto *reservations*, areas of land set aside for them. Reservations were often small and poor for farming. Government food and supplies often came late or not at all. When the buffalo herds were destroyed in the 1870s and 1880s, Plains nations lost their main source of food. Many felt they had no choice but to fight or to move onto reservations.

lessons.title: Sand Creek and Little Bighorn
lessons.mainIdea: Broken treaties led to bloody wars, including the Sand Creek Massacre in 1864 and the Lakota and Cheyenne victory at Little Bighorn in 1876.
reading: In November 1864, a camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho people was resting at Sand Creek in Colorado Territory. Their leaders believed they were at peace with the United States. One chief, Black Kettle, flew an American flag over his lodge. Colorado soldiers led by John Chivington attacked anyway. They killed more than 150 people, most of them women, children and elders. A later government investigation condemned the attack. It is now known as the Sand Creek *Massacre*.

In 1868, the Treaty of Fort Laramie promised the Black Hills to the Lakota. The Black Hills were sacred to them. But in 1874, an army expedition led by George Armstrong Custer reported gold there. Miners poured in, and the government pressured the Lakota to give up the land. Lakota and Cheyenne people who refused to move to reservations gathered around leaders such as Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse.

On June 25, 1876, Custer's soldiers attacked a large village near the Little Bighorn River in Montana. Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors fought back and killed Custer and all the soldiers with him. It was a great victory for the Plains nations, but it did not last. The army sent more troops, and within about a year most of the fighters had been forced onto reservations. The government took the Black Hills.

lessons.title: Chief Joseph and the Nez Perce
lessons.mainIdea: In 1877, the Nez Perce tried to escape to Canada rather than lose their homeland, but they were stopped just short of the border.
reading: The Nez Perce lived in the valleys of what are now Oregon, Idaho and Washington. For years they were at peace with Americans. They even helped Lewis and Clark in 1805. But settlers wanted their land. In 1877, the government ordered one band of Nez Perce, led in part by a young chief named Joseph, to leave the Wallowa Valley and move to a small reservation.

Fighting broke out after a few young Nez Perce men killed some settlers. Fearing punishment for the whole band, about 800 Nez Perce fled. For more than three months, they traveled over 1,000 miles through mountains, heading for Canada. Families, elders and children made the journey, along with their horses. Again and again they held off the soldiers who chased them.

In October 1877, the army caught up with them in Montana, only about 40 miles from the Canadian border. Cold, hungry and exhausted, Joseph and his people surrendered. They had been promised they could go home, but instead they were sent to Kansas and then to Indian Territory, where many died of disease. Joseph spent the rest of his life asking the government to let his people return to their homeland.

lessons.title: Schools and Land Allotment
lessons.mainIdea: Boarding schools and the Dawes Act tried to erase Native cultures and took away most of the land Native nations still held.
reading: By the 1880s, many reformers in the East said they wanted to help Native Americans. But their plan was *assimilation*, which meant making Native people give up their own ways and live like white Americans. The government and churches built boarding schools, often far from reservations. Children were sent there, sometimes by force.

The most famous was the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, opened in 1879. Students had their hair cut and their clothes replaced with uniforms. They were given English names and punished for speaking their own languages. Many were deeply lonely, and some died of disease far from home. Still, many students held on to their identity, and some later became leaders for their nations.

In 1887, Congress passed the *Dawes Act*. It broke up reservation land into separate plots, usually 160 acres for each head of a family. Land left over was sold to white settlers. Supporters said owning farms would help Native families. Instead, much of the land ended up in outside hands. Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million acres by 1934.

lessons.title: Wounded Knee and the End of the Frontier
lessons.mainIdea: The killing of Lakota people at Wounded Knee in 1890 ended the wars on the Plains, the same year officials said the frontier was gone.
reading: By 1890, life on the reservations was hard. Food was short, and the old ways were forbidden. Many Lakota joined a new religious movement called the *Ghost Dance*. Believers danced and prayed for a time when the buffalo would return and the settlers would leave. Government agents feared the Ghost Dance would lead to an uprising.

In December 1890, reservation police killed Sitting Bull while trying to arrest him. Soon after, soldiers stopped a band of Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota. On December 29, as soldiers took their weapons, a shot went off. The soldiers opened fire. Hundreds of Lakota men, women and children were killed. The Wounded Knee Massacre marked the end of the armed fight for the Plains.

That same year, the U.S. Census reported that there was no longer a clear *frontier* line, a border between settled and unsettled land. In 1893, at a meeting in Chicago, historian Frederick Jackson Turner argued that the frontier had shaped the American character. He said it made Americans independent and democratic. Later historians pointed out that his idea left out the Native nations who had lived on that "free land" all along.

chapters.title: Industrialization and Immigration
chapters.bigQuestion: How did factories, big business and millions of newcomers change the lives of ordinary Americans?

story.title: A House on Halsted Street
story.kicker: In 1889, two young women moved into an old mansion in one of Chicago's poorest neighborhoods and opened its doors to everyone.
paragraphs: In 1889, the neighborhood around Halsted Street on Chicago's Near West Side was crowded and noisy. Families from Italy, Greece, Russia, Poland, Ireland, Germany and many other places squeezed into wooden buildings. Streets were muddy, and garbage piled up in the alleys. Many parents worked long hours in factories and sweatshops. Their children often worked too.

That year, Jane Addams and her friend Ellen Gates Starr rented part of an old mansion in the middle of this neighborhood. It had been built years before by a man named Charles Hull, so they called it Hull House. Addams had grown up in Cedarville, Illinois, in a comfortable family. She wanted to do more than give money to the poor. She wanted to live among her neighbors and learn what they needed.

Hull House grew quickly. It opened a kindergarten and a day nursery, so working mothers had a safe place for their young children. It offered classes in English, cooking, art and music. It had clubs for boys and girls, a gym, a library and public baths. It helped build one of Chicago's early public playgrounds. Neighbors came to lectures, plays and concerts. Immigrants could keep their own traditions while learning about their new country.

Addams and the women who worked with her also pushed for changes in the law. They studied the neighborhood, house by house, and wrote about what they found. Florence Kelley, who lived at Hull House, investigated sweatshops and helped win an Illinois law limiting work hours for women and banning factory work for young children. Addams even became the garbage inspector for her ward, following the wagons at dawn to make sure the trash was collected.

Hull House became a model for hundreds of settlement houses across the country. In 1931, Jane Addams became the first American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Today, part of the original Hull House still stands as a museum on the campus of the University of Illinois Chicago. It is a reminder that big cities can also be places where neighbors take care of one another.
story.think: Jane Addams chose to live in the neighborhood instead of just giving money. Why might that have made her work more useful?

sections.title: An Age of Machines and Money

lessons.title: Steel, Oil and Electricity
lessons.mainIdea: New ways to make steel, refine oil and use electricity powered a huge growth of American industry after the Civil War.
reading: After the Civil War, the United States became an *industrial* nation, where factories and machines made more and more of what people used. Three things helped power this change: steel, oil and electricity. The country also had plenty of coal, iron, timber and workers, plus railroads to move goods.

Steel is stronger than iron, but it used to be slow and costly to make. The *Bessemer process*, developed in the 1850s, blew air through melted iron to burn out impurities. Suddenly steel could be made cheaply and in huge amounts. Steel became rails, bridges, machines and the frames of tall buildings. Pittsburgh became a great steel city, and Chicago's mills grew too.

In 1859, a well in Titusville, Pennsylvania, struck oil. At first, oil was refined into kerosene for lamps. Later, gasoline powered cars. Meanwhile, electricity began to light homes and streets and run factory machines. These new industries created millions of jobs, but many of those jobs were dangerous and poorly paid.

a method of making steel cheaply by blowing air through melted iron
to clean or change a raw material into a more useful product

lessons.title: Inventors Change Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Inventors such as Alexander Graham Bell, Thomas Edison and Lewis Latimer created new tools that changed how Americans lived and worked.
reading: In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell received a *patent* for the telephone. A patent is a government paper that says only the inventor may make and sell an invention for a set time. Within a few decades, telephones linked homes and businesses across the country. People no longer had to send a letter or telegram to talk with someone far away.

Thomas Edison set up a laboratory in Menlo Park, New Jersey, where teams of workers tested ideas day and night. Edison's lab produced the phonograph, which recorded sound, and a long-lasting light bulb in 1879. In 1882, his company opened a power station in New York City that sent electricity to nearby buildings.

Lewis Latimer, the son of parents who escaped slavery, taught himself mechanical drawing. He drew the patent drawings for Bell's telephone. Later he improved the carbon filament, the thin thread inside a light bulb that glows, helping bulbs last longer and cost less. Latimer worked for Edison's company and wrote a book about electric lighting. His story shows that Black inventors helped build the modern world.

words.d: a government paper that gives an inventor the only right to make and sell an invention for a time
the thin thread inside a light bulb that glows when electricity passes through it
a new tool, machine or process that someone creates

lessons.title: Giants of Big Business
lessons.mainIdea: Business leaders like Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller built giant companies, earning praise for their gifts and criticism for their methods.
reading: Big industries needed huge amounts of money. Many businesses became *corporations*, companies owned by many people who buy shares called stock. Some corporations grew so large that they controlled almost a whole industry. A company with no real competition is called a *monopoly*. Without competitors, it can set high prices and low wages.

Andrew Carnegie came to America from Scotland as a poor boy and worked in a cotton mill. He built a steel empire by owning every step of making steel, from iron mines to ships and railroads. John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil. He bought out or pushed aside rival refiners. By around 1880, Standard Oil controlled about 90 percent of the oil refining in the United States. Rockefeller joined companies together in a *trust*, which let a few people run them all.

People argued about these men. Critics called them robber barons. They said the owners got rich by crushing rivals and paying workers little. Supporters called them captains of industry who created jobs and cheaper goods. Both men gave away huge fortunes. Carnegie paid for more than 2,500 public libraries. Rockefeller helped start the University of Chicago. In 1890, Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act to try to break up monopolies.

words.d: a business owned by many people who buy shares of stock
a company that controls an entire industry with no real competition
a group of companies joined together and run by one board
giving money to help others and improve society

lessons.title: A New Wave of Immigrants
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1880 and 1914, millions of immigrants, many from southern and eastern Europe, came to the United States for work and freedom.
reading: Before 1880, most immigrants came from northern and western Europe, such as Ireland, Germany and Britain. After 1880, more and more came from southern and eastern Europe: Italy, Greece, Poland, Russia and Austria-Hungary. Others came from China, Japan, Mexico, the Caribbean and the Middle East. Historians call this the era of the *new immigrants*.

People left home for many reasons. These are called *push factors*: poverty, lack of land, hunger, and persecution. Jews in the Russian Empire faced violent attacks called pogroms. *Pull factors* drew people to America: jobs in factories and mines, cheap land, freedom of religion, and letters from relatives who had already made the trip.

Most immigrants crossed the ocean crowded below deck in steamships. Once here, many settled in cities near others from their homeland. They built churches, synagogues, newspapers, mutual aid clubs and shops. Chicago became home to large Polish, Italian, Czech, Swedish, German and Irish communities. Immigrants did much of the hard work that built American cities and industries.

words.d: immigrants who came mainly from southern and eastern Europe after about 1880
a problem that makes people want to leave their home

lessons.title: Through the Golden Door
lessons.mainIdea: Immigrants from Europe passed through Ellis Island, while many Asian immigrants faced long waits and harsh questioning at Angel Island.
reading: Starting in 1892, most European immigrants arriving in New York passed through *Ellis Island*, near the Statue of Liberty. Doctors checked them for disease. Officials asked their names, jobs and where they were going. For most, the process took a few hours. Only about 2 percent were turned away, usually for illness. Millions of Americans today have an ancestor who passed through Ellis Island.

On the West Coast, many immigrants arrived at *Angel Island* in San Francisco Bay, which opened in 1910. Most were from China. Because of laws that kept most Chinese people out, officials questioned them for days about tiny details of their families and villages. Some were held for weeks or even months.

While they waited, some Chinese detainees carved poems into the wooden walls. The poems speak of loneliness, anger and hope. Many of them can still be read today. Angel Island also processed immigrants from Japan, Korea, India, Mexico, Russia and other countries.

an immigration station in San Francisco Bay that opened in 1910

lessons.title: Closing the Door to Chinese Immigrants
lessons.mainIdea: In 1882, the Chinese Exclusion Act became the first U.S. law to ban immigrants because of their nationality.
reading: Chinese immigrants had worked in the gold fields and built the Central Pacific Railroad. Many opened laundries, restaurants and farms. But some white workers blamed them for low wages and lost jobs. This feeling against immigrants is called *nativism*. In the West, Chinese people faced unfair taxes, riots and attacks.

In 1882, Congress passed the *Chinese Exclusion Act*. It stopped Chinese workers from entering the country and kept Chinese immigrants already here from becoming citizens. It was the first major U.S. law to shut out people because of their nationality. It was later renewed and made permanent. It was not repealed until 1943, during World War II, when China was an American ally.

Chinese Americans fought back in court. Wong Kim Ark was born in San Francisco to Chinese parents. When he returned from a trip to China, officials tried to keep him out. In 1898, the Supreme Court ruled that because he was born in the United States, he was a citizen under the 14th Amendment. That ruling still protects the citizenship of people born in the United States.

an 1882 law that stopped most Chinese immigrants from coming to the U.S.

lessons.title: Chicago Rises from the Ashes
lessons.mainIdea: American cities grew at amazing speed, and Chicago rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1871 to become a leader in tall buildings.
reading: Factories needed workers, and workers needed homes. People poured into cities from farms and from other countries. In the crowded parts of town, families lived in *tenements*, cheap apartment buildings with small, dark rooms. Many had little fresh air, no bathrooms inside and a real danger of fire and disease.

In October 1871, a fire broke out on Chicago's West Side. Strong winds pushed it across the city. The Great Chicago Fire burned for about two days. It killed about 300 people and left about 100,000 homeless. Much of downtown was destroyed. Chicagoans rebuilt fast, this time with more brick, stone and iron.

In the 1880s, Chicago architects began building *skyscrapers*, tall buildings held up by frames of iron and steel instead of thick walls. The Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885, is often called the first skyscraper. Safe elevators made tall buildings practical. Electric streetcars let people live farther from work. In 1893, Chicago showed off its new strength by hosting a huge world's fair, the World's Columbian Exposition.

a very tall building held up by a steel frame

lessons.title: Helping Hands and Party Bosses
lessons.mainIdea: Settlement houses and political machines both helped city newcomers, but machines often traded help for votes and were often corrupt.
reading: Crowded cities had many problems: dirty water, garbage, crime and fire. Two very different groups stepped in to help newcomers. One was the *settlement house*, a center where reformers lived in a poor neighborhood and offered classes, child care and other help. Hull House in Chicago was the best known. By 1900, there were about a hundred settlement houses across the country.

The other was the *political machine*, a group that controlled a city's government. A machine was led by a boss. Its workers found immigrants jobs, gave families coal in winter and helped people in trouble with the law. In return, they expected votes. The most famous machine was Tammany Hall in New York City.

Machines were often *corrupt*. Bosses took bribes and gave city contracts to friends at high prices. New York's Boss William Tweed and his friends stole millions of dollars from the city before he was sent to prison in the 1870s. Reformers wanted to replace machines with honest, well-run city governments.

sections.title: Workers and the Fight for Fairness

lessons.title: Long Days and Small Hands
lessons.mainIdea: Factory workers, including many children, faced long hours, low pay and danger, so they formed labor unions to demand better conditions.
reading: Factory jobs were hard. Many people worked 10 to 12 hours a day, six days a week. Machines had no safety guards, and injuries were common. If a worker was hurt, there was usually no pay while they healed. Wages were so low that whole families had to work, including children.

By 1900, well over a million children under 16 had jobs. Children worked in textile mills, coal mines, canneries and city streets. Their small hands could fix threads on spinning machines or sort coal. They missed school, and many were injured or became sick. *Child labor* became one of the biggest issues of the era.

Workers joined together in *labor unions* to bargain as a group. The Knights of Labor, founded in 1869, welcomed almost all workers, including women and Black workers. In 1886, Samuel Gompers helped start the American Federation of Labor (AFL), which brought together unions of skilled workers. Unions pushed for higher pay, safer shops and the eight-hour day. When talks failed, workers might go on *strike*, refusing to work until their demands were met.

lessons.title: Haymarket and Pullman
lessons.mainIdea: Two conflicts in the Chicago area, the Haymarket affair of 1886 and the Pullman Strike of 1894, showed how bitter the fight between workers and owners became.
reading: In May 1886, workers across the country marched for an eight-hour workday. In Chicago, police shot and killed strikers near the McCormick Reaper Works. On May 4, workers held a protest rally at Haymarket Square. As police moved in to break it up, someone threw a bomb. Police officers and people in the crowd were killed. No one ever proved who threw the bomb.

Eight men with *anarchist* ideas, who believed in getting rid of government, were convicted. Four were hanged. Many people blamed unions for the violence, and the Knights of Labor lost members. In 1893, Illinois Governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned the three men still in prison. He said their trial had been unfair.

George Pullman built railroad sleeping cars. His workers lived in Pullman, a company town just south of Chicago. In 1894, during hard times, he cut wages but did not lower rents. Workers went on strike. The American Railway Union, led by Eugene Debs, refused to handle trains with Pullman cars, and rail traffic across much of the country stopped. President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops, a court ordered the strike to end, and Debs went to jail. The strike was crushed.

lessons.title: Separate and Unequal
lessons.mainIdea: After Reconstruction, Jim Crow laws and the Plessy decision made segregation legal, and Ida B. Wells bravely exposed racial violence.
reading: In the South, states passed *Jim Crow* laws that separated Black and white people in schools, trains, parks and restaurants. This separation is called *segregation*. States also used poll taxes and unfair tests to stop Black men from voting. In the North, segregation was often not written into law, but Black Americans still faced unfair treatment in jobs and housing.

In 1892, Homer Plessy, a man of mixed race, sat in a whites-only train car in Louisiana to test the law. He was arrested. In 1896, in Plessy v. Ferguson, the Supreme Court ruled that segregation was legal as long as facilities were "separate but equal." In real life, facilities for Black Americans were almost never equal. Only one justice, John Marshall Harlan, disagreed.

Ida B. Wells was a journalist born into slavery in Mississippi. After three of her friends were murdered by a mob in Memphis, she began to investigate *lynching*, the killing of people by mobs without a trial. She showed that lynching was a tool of terror, not justice. Threatened with death, she moved north and later settled in Chicago, where she kept writing, organizing and fighting for equal rights.

words.d: laws and customs that kept Black and white Americans separate and unequal
keeping people apart by race
the murder of a person by a mob, without a trial

lessons.title: Two Paths Toward Equality
lessons.mainIdea: Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois disagreed about how Black Americans should win equality, and Du Bois helped found the NAACP in 1909.
reading: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery in Virginia. He became head of the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, a school that trained Black students in trades, farming and teaching. In an 1895 speech in Atlanta, Washington said Black Americans should build skills and wealth first, and not push hard for social equality right away. Many white leaders praised his view.

W.E.B. Du Bois was born free in Massachusetts and was the first Black American to earn a PhD from Harvard. He disagreed with Washington. Du Bois said Black Americans should demand full rights now, including voting rights and a good education. He believed a talented group of educated leaders should lead the fight. In 1903, he wrote The Souls of Black Folk.

In 1909, Du Bois, Ida B. Wells, Jane Addams and others helped found the *NAACP*, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It used lawsuits, protests and its magazine, The Crisis, which Du Bois edited, to fight *discrimination*. The NAACP would win major court cases in the decades that followed.

chapters.title: The Progressive Era
chapters.bigQuestion: How did Americans try to fix the problems of a fast-changing country, and how far did they reach beyond their borders?

story.title: Saving the Wild Places
story.kicker: A nation that had spent a century taming the land began to ask a new question: which places should be kept wild forever?
paragraphs: In 1870, a group of explorers rode into a strange land in the Rocky Mountains. They saw hot springs in bright colors, boiling mud pots and a geyser that shot water high into the air, again and again, like clockwork. They named that geyser Old Faithful. The explorers worried that private owners would fence in these wonders and charge people to see them.

In 1872, Congress set aside Yellowstone, in the Rocky Mountains of Wyoming Territory, as a public park "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people." President Ulysses S. Grant signed the law. Yellowstone became the first national park in the world. The land was not empty, though. Native peoples, including the Shoshone, Crow and others, had hunted and gathered there for thousands of years. Over time they were pushed out of the park.

Out in California, a Scottish-born writer named John Muir fell in love with the Sierra Nevada mountains and Yosemite Valley. He wrote about giant sequoia trees and granite cliffs as if they were holy places. His writing helped convince Congress to create Yosemite National Park in 1890. In 1892, Muir helped start the Sierra Club to protect wild lands. Around 1900, Black soldiers of the U.S. Army, known as Buffalo Soldiers, patrolled Yosemite and Sequoia to stop illegal grazing and logging. In 1903, Captain Charles Young became the first Black leader of a national park.

That same year, President Theodore Roosevelt went camping with Muir in Yosemite. They slept under the stars and talked about saving forests. Roosevelt had loved the outdoors since he was a sickly boy. As president, he protected about 230 million acres of public land as national forests, parks, wildlife refuges and monuments. In 1906, he used a new law, the Antiquities Act, to make Devils Tower in Wyoming the first national monument.

By 1916, the country had many national parks and monuments, but no one agency ran them. That year, President Woodrow Wilson signed a law creating the National Park Service. Its job was to protect the parks and let people enjoy them, now and in the future. Today, there are more than 60 national parks. Their story raises a question people still debate: how should we balance using the land with saving it?
story.think: National parks protected wild places, but Native peoples who had lived there were pushed out. How can we tell the story of the parks in a way that is fair to everyone?

lessons.title: Reporters Who Dug Up the Truth
lessons.mainIdea: Progressive reformers and journalists called muckrakers exposed problems in cities, business and government so that the public would demand change.
reading: Around 1900, many Americans believed the country needed fixing. Cities were crowded and dirty. Big businesses had huge power. Governments were often corrupt. People who wanted to use government and science to solve these problems were called *Progressives*. They came from both major parties and many walks of life.

Some of the most important Progressives were writers. Theodore Roosevelt called them *muckrakers*, after a character in an old book who was always raking up dirt. He meant it partly as a complaint, but the writers wore the name with pride. Their job was to dig up hidden facts and tell the public.

Jacob Riis, a Danish immigrant, used a camera and flash powder to photograph dark tenements in New York. His 1890 book How the Other Half Lives shocked readers. Ida Tarbell spent years studying Standard Oil. Her articles, published between 1902 and 1904, showed how Rockefeller had crushed rivals. Lincoln Steffens wrote about corrupt city governments. Their work led to new laws and reforms.

words.d: a reformer of the early 1900s who wanted government to fix social and economic problems
a journalist who exposed wrongdoing in business or government
a change made to improve something

look.title: The Power of a Photograph
look.text: Many wealthy New Yorkers had never walked through a tenement. Jacob Riis's flash photographs showed them children sleeping in hallways and families crowded into tiny rooms without windows.
look.prompt: Why might a photograph change people's minds more than a written report? Can you think of a photo from today that did the same?

choices: Exposed wrongdoing in business and government
check.why: Muckrakers were journalists who dug up and published hidden problems.

check.q: What did Jacob Riis use to show how poor New Yorkers lived?
check.why: Riis photographed crowded tenements in How the Other Half Lives (1890).

check.q: Which company did Ida Tarbell investigate?
check.why: Tarbell's articles showed how Standard Oil crushed its competitors.

lessons.title: The Jungle and Safer Food
lessons.mainIdea: Upton Sinclair's novel about Chicago's meatpacking plants led Congress to pass the first national food safety laws in 1906.
reading: Chicago's Union Stock Yards were the center of the nation's meat industry. Thousands of workers, many of them immigrants from Lithuania, Poland and other lands, worked in the packinghouses nearby. The work was fast, dangerous and poorly paid.

In 1906, Upton Sinclair published *The Jungle*, a novel about a Lithuanian immigrant family in Chicago's packinghouse district. Sinclair wanted readers to care about the workers. But readers were most shocked by what the book said about the meat itself: rats, filth and spoiled meat mixed into products sold to the public. Sales of meat dropped.

President Theodore Roosevelt sent inspectors to Chicago. They found many of the problems were real. In 1906, Congress passed the *Meat Inspection Act*, which required government inspectors to check meat. It also passed the *Pure Food and Drug Act*, which banned harmful or falsely labeled foods and medicines. These laws were the start of the government's role in keeping food and medicine safe.

words.d: a 1906 novel by Upton Sinclair about workers in Chicago's meatpacking plants
a 1906 law requiring government inspection of meat
a 1906 law banning harmful or falsely labeled food and medicine

look.text: I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach.

choices: An immigrant family working in Chicago's meatpacking plants

lessons.title: Giving Voters More Power
lessons.mainIdea: Progressives changed state and national government so that ordinary voters, not party bosses, had more control.
reading: Progressives believed that party bosses and big businesses had too much control over government. Their answer was to give voters more direct power. One step was the secret ballot, so voters could choose in private without being pressured. Another was the *direct primary*, an election in which voters, not party leaders, choose a party's candidates.

Wisconsin, led by Governor Robert La Follette, became a model of Progressive reform. Other states, such as Oregon, adopted three new tools. The *initiative* lets citizens propose a law by gathering signatures. The *referendum* lets voters approve or reject a law directly. The *recall* lets voters remove an elected official before the term ends.

Before 1913, U.S. senators were chosen by state legislatures, which party bosses and wealthy interests could sway. The *17th Amendment*, ratified in 1913, let voters in each state elect their senators directly. Progressives also worked to improve city government by hiring trained experts to run services like water and garbage collection.

a way for citizens to propose a new law by collecting signatures
a vote in which citizens approve or reject a law
a vote to remove an elected official from office early

lessons.title: Roosevelt's Square Deal
lessons.mainIdea: Theodore Roosevelt used the power of the presidency to control big business and give workers and consumers what he called a Square Deal.
reading: In 1901, President William McKinley was shot and killed. Vice President Theodore Roosevelt, only 42 years old, became the youngest president in the nation's history. Roosevelt was full of energy. He believed the president should act boldly for the public good. He promised Americans a *Square Deal*, meaning fair treatment for business owners, workers and consumers alike.

Roosevelt did not think all big businesses were bad. But he believed "bad trusts" that harmed the public should be broken up. In 1904, the Supreme Court agreed with his government that a giant railroad company, Northern Securities, broke the Sherman Antitrust Act. Roosevelt's government brought dozens of lawsuits against trusts. People called him a *trustbuster*.

In 1902, coal miners in Pennsylvania went on strike. As winter came, people feared they would have no coal to heat their homes. Past presidents had sent troops to break strikes. Roosevelt instead brought both sides to the White House and pushed them to accept a settlement. Miners won higher pay and shorter hours. It was the first time a president stepped in as a neutral judge in a labor dispute.

words.d: Theodore Roosevelt's promise of fair treatment for business, workers and consumers
a person who breaks up trusts and monopolies
a person who buys and uses goods and services

look.title: Good Trusts and Bad Trusts
look.text: Roosevelt said a large company was fine if it made good products at fair prices. He said the government should break up a company only if it used its size to cheat customers, crush rivals or harm workers.
look.prompt: Do you agree that size alone does not make a company bad? What would make a company harmful to the public?

check.why: Roosevelt was vice president and took office when McKinley was shot and killed.

choices: Fair treatment for business, workers and consumers

check.why: The Square Deal promised fairness for all sides of the economy.

check.why: Roosevelt brought both sides together and pushed them to a settlement, a first for a president.

lessons.title: Using and Saving the Land
lessons.mainIdea: Roosevelt and other conservationists protected millions of acres, but Americans disagreed about whether to use natural resources wisely or leave wild places untouched.
reading: By 1900, loggers had cut down huge forests, and hunters had wiped out or nearly wiped out several kinds of animals. Roosevelt believed natural resources belonged to the whole nation, including future generations. This idea is called *conservation*. In 1905, the U.S. Forest Service was created, led by Gifford Pinchot.

Pinchot and John Muir were both conservationists, but they disagreed. Pinchot believed in "wise use." Forests, rivers and grasslands should be used for timber, water and grazing, but carefully, so they would last. Muir believed in *preservation*. Some wild places should be left untouched, protected for their beauty and for nature itself.

Their biggest fight was over Hetch Hetchy, a valley inside Yosemite National Park. The growing city of San Francisco wanted to dam the valley to supply water. Muir fought hard to save it. Pinchot supported the dam. In 1913, Congress approved it, and the valley was flooded. The debate between using land and preserving it continues today.

words.d: the careful use and protection of natural resources
keeping wild places untouched and protected
something from nature that people use, such as water, trees or minerals

choices: Selling public land to private companies

choices: Muir wanted some places left untouched; Pinchot wanted careful use

check.why: Muir favored preservation, while Pinchot favored wise use of resources.

choices: It became the first national park

lessons.title: Taft, Wilson and New Laws
lessons.mainIdea: Presidents Taft and Wilson continued Progressive reform, adding an income tax, the Federal Reserve and stronger rules for business.
reading: William Howard Taft, Roosevelt's chosen successor, became president in 1909. Taft actually brought more antitrust lawsuits than Roosevelt did. In 1911, the Supreme Court broke up Standard Oil. But Taft sided with more conservative Republicans on some issues, and Roosevelt grew angry. In 1912, Roosevelt ran against Taft as the candidate of a new Progressive Party, nicknamed the Bull Moose Party.

The split among Republicans helped Democrat Woodrow Wilson win. Wilson called his plan the New Freedom. In 1913, the *16th Amendment* allowed Congress to collect an income tax. That same year, Congress created the *Federal Reserve*, a system of banks that manages the nation's money supply. In 1914, the Clayton Antitrust Act strengthened the rules against monopolies and protected unions' right to strike, and the Federal Trade Commission was set up to stop unfair business practices.

Progressive reform had limits. Many Progressives cared little about the rights of Black Americans. Wilson allowed several federal departments to segregate their Black and white workers. Black leaders who had hoped for fair treatment protested strongly.

words.d: the 1913 change to the Constitution that allows a federal income tax
a tax on the money people earn
the nation's central banking system, which manages the money supply

lessons.title: A Long Road to the Ballot
lessons.mainIdea: Women fought for the right to vote for more than 70 years, winning first in western states and in Illinois before the national victory.
reading: The fight for woman *suffrage*, or women's right to vote, began at Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848. After the Civil War, many suffragists were angry that the 15th Amendment protected Black men's voting rights but said nothing about women. In 1869, Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton formed a group to push for a constitutional amendment.

In 1872, Susan B. Anthony voted in the presidential election in Rochester, New York. She was arrested, tried and fined $100. She refused to pay. Anthony traveled the country giving speeches for decades. She died in 1906, before women won the vote nationally, but the 19th Amendment would later be nicknamed the Susan B. Anthony Amendment.

Change came first in the West. Wyoming Territory gave women the vote in 1869. By 1914, most western states had followed. In 1913, Illinois let women vote for president and in many local elections, the first state east of the Mississippi River to do so. That year, Ida B. Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club in Chicago to help Black women use their new votes.

words.d: the right to vote
a person who worked to win voting rights for women
a change or addition to the Constitution

look.cite: Susan B. Anthony, speech after her arrest for voting, 1873

choices: Her vote was counted with no problem

lessons.title: Winning the 19th Amendment
lessons.mainIdea: Using both quiet persuasion and bold protest, suffragists won the 19th Amendment in 1920, though many women of color still faced barriers to voting.
reading: By the 1910s, suffragists used two different plans. Carrie Chapman Catt led the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Her "Winning Plan" worked state by state while also pressing Congress. She believed in patient, polite persuasion. Alice Paul, a younger leader, chose bolder action. Her group, later called the National Woman's Party, held parades and *protests* to get attention.

In 1917, Alice Paul's group began picketing outside the White House. The women, called the Silent Sentinels, held signs asking President Wilson how he could fight for democracy abroad while women at home could not vote. Many were arrested and jailed. When some went on a hunger strike, guards force-fed them. News of this treatment won the suffragists public sympathy.

Women's work during World War I also strengthened their case. Wilson came to support suffrage. Congress passed the *19th Amendment* in 1919, and it was ratified in August 1920, when Tennessee became the 36th state to approve it. Still, many Black women in the South were kept from voting by Jim Crow laws. Many Native American women could not vote because they were not yet treated as citizens.

a public action to show strong disagreement
to stand outside a place with signs as a protest

lessons.title: Why America Looked Outward
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s, the United States began to gain lands overseas, including Alaska and Hawaii, in a push called imperialism.
reading: European nations were racing to build *empires* by taking control of lands in Africa and Asia. This practice is called *imperialism*. Many American leaders wanted the United States to join the race. Businesses wanted new markets for their goods. Naval officer Alfred Thayer Mahan argued that a great nation needed a strong navy and bases around the world. Some Americans also believed, wrongly, that their culture was better than others and should be spread.

In 1867, Secretary of State William Seward bought Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million. Critics mocked the deal as "Seward's Folly." Their view changed when gold and other riches were found there. Alaska later became a state in 1959.

Hawaii was an independent kingdom. American planters grew rich there growing sugar. In 1893, the planters overthrew Queen Liliuokalani with help from U.S. Marines. The queen gave up her power under protest to avoid bloodshed. The United States annexed Hawaii in 1898. Many Native Hawaiians opposed the takeover, and in 1993 Congress formally apologized for the overthrow.

a group of lands and peoples ruled by one powerful nation
to add a territory to a country

lessons.title: War with Spain
lessons.mainIdea: In 1898, the United States fought a short war with Spain that began over Cuba and ended with the U.S. gaining Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.
reading: Cuba, an island just 90 miles from Florida, was a Spanish colony. In 1895, Cubans rose up to fight for independence. Spain fought back harshly, forcing many Cubans into crowded camps where many died. American newspapers printed shocking and sometimes exaggerated stories. This style of sensational reporting was called *yellow journalism*.

In February 1898, the U.S. battleship Maine exploded in the harbor of Havana, Cuba, and more than 250 sailors died. The cause was never proven, but many Americans blamed Spain. "Remember the Maine!" became a rallying cry. In April 1898, the United States declared war.

The war lasted only a few months. Commodore George Dewey's ships destroyed a Spanish fleet in Manila Bay in the Philippines. In Cuba, Theodore Roosevelt's volunteer Rough Riders and Black soldiers of the 9th and 10th Cavalry fought at San Juan Hill. In the peace treaty, Spain gave the United States Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. Cuba became independent, but the U.S. kept the right to step into its affairs.

words.d: news reporting that uses shocking and exaggerated stories to sell papers
a land ruled by another country
a volunteer cavalry unit led by Theodore Roosevelt in the Spanish-American War

look.title: Headlines and War
look.text: Some newspapers competed to sell the most copies. They printed huge headlines and dramatic drawings about Spanish cruelty in Cuba and blamed Spain for the Maine explosion before anyone knew the cause.
look.prompt: How can news reports push a country toward war? How can readers today check whether a story is exaggerated?

check.q: What was yellow journalism?
choices: Shocking, exaggerated news stories used to sell papers
check.why: Yellow journalism used sensational stories to attract readers.

check.q: What event helped push the U.S. into war with Spain in 1898?
choices: The explosion of the USS Maine in Havana harbor
check.why: The Maine exploded in February 1898, and many Americans blamed Spain.

check.q: Which lands did the United States gain from Spain in 1898?
choices: Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines
check.why: The peace treaty gave the U.S. Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

lessons.title: The Philippines and the Debate over Empire
lessons.mainIdea: When the U.S. took the Philippines, Filipinos fought for independence, and Americans argued over whether their country should rule other peoples.
reading: Filipinos had been fighting Spain for their independence. Their leader, Emilio Aguinaldo, expected freedom when Spain lost. Instead, the United States took control of the islands. In 1899, war broke out between Filipino fighters and American troops. The *Philippine-American War* lasted about three years of major fighting and cost many more lives than the war with Spain, most of them Filipino.

At home, Americans argued. Supporters of the new empire said the islands would help trade and the navy. Some said Americans had a duty to govern the Filipinos. The *Anti-Imperialist League* strongly disagreed. Its members included writer Mark Twain and Jane Addams of Hull House. They said ruling people without their consent went against the Declaration of Independence.

The United States ruled the Philippines for decades. It built schools and roads, but Filipinos were not free to govern themselves. The Philippines finally became independent in 1946. Puerto Rico and Guam remain U.S. territories today. People born in Puerto Rico have been U.S. citizens since 1917.

words.d: the war between Filipino fighters and U.S. troops that began in 1899
a group of Americans who opposed taking overseas colonies
permission or agreement
an area ruled by the U.S. that is not a state

look.title: Consent of the Governed
look.text: The Declaration of Independence says governments get their power "from the consent of the governed." In 1899, the United States governed millions of Filipinos who had not agreed to its rule and who were fighting for their own independence.
look.prompt: How did anti-imperialists use the Declaration to argue against ruling the Philippines? How might supporters of the empire have answered?

check.q: Why did Filipinos fight the United States after 1898?
choices: They wanted independence, not a new ruler
They wanted to become part of Spain again
They wanted to join the Anti-Imperialist League
The U.S. had refused to trade with them
check.why: Filipinos expected independence after Spain lost, but the United States took control.

check.q: What did the Anti-Imperialist League argue?
choices: Ruling people without their consent went against American ideals
The U.S. should take even more colonies
The Philippines should be sold back to Spain
Only the navy should decide foreign policy
check.why: Anti-imperialists said colonies went against the Declaration's idea of consent of the governed.

check.q: When did the Philippines become independent?
check.why: The Philippines gained full independence from the United States in 1946.

lessons.title: A Canal and a Big Stick
lessons.mainIdea: Theodore Roosevelt helped Panama break from Colombia, built the Panama Canal, and claimed the right for the U.S. to police Latin America.
reading: Ships going from New York to San Francisco had to sail all the way around South America. A canal across Central America would save weeks. The best route crossed Panama, which was then part of Colombia. When Colombia refused Roosevelt's offer, Panamanian rebels declared independence in 1903. U.S. warships helped keep Colombia from stopping them. The new nation quickly gave the United States the right to build a canal.

Building the Panama Canal took ten years, from 1904 to 1914. Workers dug through mountains and jungle. Diseases spread by mosquitoes, yellow fever and malaria, had killed thousands during an earlier French attempt. Dr. William Gorgas led a campaign to drain swamps and kill mosquitoes, which saved many lives. Tens of thousands of workers, many from Barbados, Jamaica and other Caribbean islands, did the hardest and most dangerous jobs. Thousands died.

Roosevelt believed the United States should be a strong power in its own region. In 1904, he announced the *Roosevelt Corollary* to the Monroe Doctrine. It said the U.S. could step in to Latin American countries that could not keep order or pay their debts. The U.S. later sent troops to several Caribbean and Central American countries. Many Latin Americans resented this *intervention*.

words.d: a waterway across Panama that connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, opened in 1914
Roosevelt's 1904 claim that the U.S. could step into Latin American nations' affairs
when one country gets involved in another country's affairs

look.title: Speak Softly
look.text: I have always been fond of the West African proverb: "Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far."
look.prompt: What does the "big stick" stand for? How did Roosevelt's actions in Panama fit this idea?

check.q: Why did the United States want a canal across Central America?
choices: To create a border with Mexico
To save ships a long trip around South America
To bring water to farms in Texas
To connect the Great Lakes to the ocean
check.why: A canal let ships move between the Atlantic and Pacific without sailing around South America.

check.q: What problem did William Gorgas help solve?
check.why: Gorgas worked to kill mosquitoes that spread yellow fever and malaria.

check.q: What did the Roosevelt Corollary claim?
choices: The U.S. could step into the affairs of Latin American countries
The U.S. would never send troops abroad
Latin America should join the United States
Europe could take colonies in Latin America
check.why: The Corollary claimed a U.S. right to intervene in Latin America.

review.q: Which book led to the Meat Inspection Act of 1906?
review.why: Upton Sinclair's The Jungle exposed conditions in Chicago's meatpacking plants.

review.q: What did the Progressives mainly believe?
choices: Government should do nothing about business
Only party bosses should choose candidates
The United States should end all elections
Government should act to fix social and economic problems
review.why: Progressives wanted government to solve problems caused by fast growth.

review.q: Which amendment gave women the right to vote?
review.why: The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, protected women's right to vote.

review.q: Which president was called a trustbuster and started the Square Deal?
review.why: Theodore Roosevelt sued trusts and promised a Square Deal.

review.q: What was the first national park in the world?
review.why: Congress created Yellowstone National Park in 1872.

review.q: How did the 17th Amendment make government more democratic?
choices: It let voters elect senators directly
review.why: Voters, instead of state legislatures, began choosing senators.

review.q: Which of these was a result of the Spanish-American War?
choices: The U.S. gained Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines
review.why: Spain handed over Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines in the peace treaty.

review.q: Why did many Latin Americans resent the Roosevelt Corollary?
choices: It closed the Panama Canal to them
It claimed the U.S. could interfere in their countries
It gave their land to Spain
review.why: The Corollary claimed a U.S. right to intervene, which many saw as a threat to their independence.
